newsitem.title: GERMANY: Long road before German tax reform becomes law.
newsitem.headline: Long road before German tax reform becomes law.

text.p: Germany's coalition tax reform, hailed by Finance Minister Theo Waigel as the biggest in post-war history, faces several rounds of horse-trading before it becomes law, Finance Ministry officials said on Thursday.
The three parties in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition were due on Thursday to give their blessing to the two-stage reform, which would take effect in 1998 and 1999.
That decision would put the ball back in the court of the Finance Ministry, whose officials would by March draw up a policy document on the reform, which should cut taxes by 30 billion marks overall.

Then, Germany's special brand of consensus politics will take proposals for scrutiny by federal states and municipalities and lobby groups representing employers, workers taxpayers and other interest groups.
A legislative draft covering the main part of the reform will then be approved by Kohl's cabinet some time in May before being introduced to both houses of parliament.
Parliamentary consultations on the legislation are expected to be lengthy, with hearings in the finance committee alone likely to last for weeks.

Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who can veto some tax legislation through their majority in the upper house of parliament, threaten to block a likely increase in value-added tax planned to offset cuts in direct taxation.
The Finance Ministry officials said that legislation is not likely to pass parliament until the autumn -- even if there are no objections in the Bundesrat upper house.
Rejection of tax measures in the upper house would then lead to parliament's mediation process being invoked -- taking political consultations through to the end of the year and possibly into 1998.

Despite the risks that the tax-cutting plan could be watered down, Hermann Otto Solms, chief tax negotiator for the Free Democrats (FDP) -- junior partners in Kohl's coalition -- said he expected the reform's main points to remain intact.
"Even if legislation is passed at the beginning of 1998, there will still be time for tax offices and companies to adjust to the new tax system," he told reporters.

Separate legislation will be brought to cut the so-called solidarity surcharge -- a levy raised to finance aid to eastern Germany -- to 5.5 percent from 7.5 percent in 1998. The bill would also cover initial reductions in taxes on corporate profits and commercial incomes.
